title: The Federalist Papers
hook: To sell a skeptical public on the new Constitution, three founders wrote 85 newspaper essays under a single fake name. They're still the best guide to what it means.
key_points: The Federalist is a series of 85 essays (1787–88) by Alexander Hamilton, James Madison, and John Jay, all published under the pen name 'Publius.'
Their immediate goal was practical: persuade New York and other states to ratify the proposed U.S. Constitution.
Federalist No. 10 argues a large republic best controls the danger of 'factions'; No. 51 explains checks and balances.
Because the authors helped design the system, courts and scholars still cite the essays as evidence of the framers' intent.
They show ratification was a public argument that had to be won — not a foregone conclusion.
content_html: When the draft Constitution went to the states in 1787, its approval was anything but certain — many Americans feared a strong central government. The most influential answer to those fears arrived as a flurry of newspaper essays signed "Publius," the joint pen name of three men who would help shape the republic.
extra_html: As political scientist Jordan Cash writes in The Conversation, The Federalist — 85 essays published in 1787–88 by Alexander Hamilton, James Madison, and John Jay — was written to persuade a wary public, especially in New York, to ratify the proposed Constitution. It doubled as a deep explanation of how the new system was meant to work. Two essays remain especially famous: Federalist No. 10, where Madison argues that a large, diverse republic is the best defense against the tyranny of "factions," and No. 51, which lays out why dividing power among branches that check one another guards against abuse — "ambition must be made to counteract ambition." Because the authors helped design the system, courts and scholars still turn to The Federalist as evidence of the framers' intent. Its deeper lesson is that the Constitution was not handed down but argued into existence — ratification was a public debate that had to be won. (U.S. founding context.)

related.title: What a Constitution Is
related.hook: The rulebook above the rules: a constitution sets out how a government is structured and the limits on its power.

related.title: Separation of Powers
related.hook: Split government into branches that make, enforce, and interpret the law — so no single part can do all three.

related.title: Key Political Thinkers
related.hook: A handful of thinkers, writing across two millennia, still frame the questions we argue about: who should rule, why obey, and how to stop power going bad?

related.title: The Declaration of Independence
related.hook: It's remembered for 'life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness' — but most of the Declaration is a long list of grievances: a case that a government had broken faith with the governed.

flashcards.prompt: What were the Federalist Papers written to do?
flashcards.back_html: Persuade the public — especially in New York — to ratify the proposed U.S. Constitution, while explaining how the new system would work.

flashcards.prompt: Who wrote the Federalist Papers, and under what name?

choices.text: Hamilton, Madison, and Jay, all writing as 'Publius'
George Washington, under his own name

flashcards.explanation_html: The three authors shared the single pen name Publius across all 85 essays.

flashcards.prompt: What is the central argument of Federalist No. 10?

choices.text: A large republic is the best way to control the danger of factions
The states should keep most power and the national government little
A single strong executive should rule without checks

flashcards.explanation_html: Madison argued that a large, diverse republic dilutes any single faction's power, guarding against majority tyranny.
